_meta.why_v2: Ground-up rebuild, installed from an owner-supplied rewrite per audit/REWRITE-INSTALL-KIT.md. Replaces a nine-plus-field micro-task generator (quick modes, an energy-level slider driving task count/complexity, habit stacking, an accountability partner, a reorder action, a raw anthropic.messages.create call with hand-rolled JSON repair, and 25-task gamified lists with points and momentum checkpoints) with one job: find ONE useful foothold in an overwhelming project, sized to the time the visitor actually has right now.
_meta.why_v3_core_reasoning: 2026-09-13, owner-supplied CONTRACT replacement. v2 reasoned from 'make it small' — a first move sized to the time budget and not fake progress, but nothing forced the model to identify what was actually BLOCKING the visitor before picking a move, so it could (and on the pricing-decision case below, would have) default to a plain task-size-reducer no different in spirit from the old design. v3 requires reasoning through: what makes the project difficult to begin (missing information / an unresolved decision / unclear scope / too many simultaneous choices / an irreversible decision faced too early / lack of usable structure / excessive size) BEFORE choosing a foothold, then requires the foothold to pass a 'so what is now better' test — completing it must leave something specific and statable easier, not just 'the visitor has started.' All old language about micro-tasks, five-minute actions, momentum, and quick wins was deliberately removed — the owner's framing: that language is what let the model default to ceremonial busywork (open the document, write the title, set a timer) over real progress. The pricing-decision case is the clearest before/after: the actual blocker is an undecided pricing model needing escalation to specific stakeholders, not a lack of task breakdown — v3 correctly surfaces and escalates the decision instead of proposing generic pricing-page busywork.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run cases (npm run check:golden task-avalanche-breaker). Diff for QUALITY not exact match: HTTP 200, no truncation, after_that capped at 3. GUARDS: validateResult() in backend/routes/task-avalanche-breaker.js requires a non-empty first_move.action (returns null / 500 otherwise), caps after_that at 3 and drops any item missing an action. The CORE REASONING discipline itself — identify the real blocker before choosing, SMALLEST MEANINGFUL PROGRESS not smallest possible action, the SO WHAT test, rejecting ceremonial actions (open the document / write the title / set a timer) unless genuinely load-bearing for this project, no diagnosis, no invented blockers, no promised momentum — is prompt-enforced (CONTRACT), not code-checkable. When eyeballing new captures: (1) does why_this name a SPECIFIC thing that becomes true, or could it accompany almost any project? (2) for a project whose real blocker is a decision/unknown/prerequisite rather than pure size, does the model surface THAT rather than defaulting to a generic organizing action? (3) is if_too_hard a genuine smaller version of the same move, not a different easier gesture? Verified live in German (de) for truncation/JSON-validity headroom — clean, correct du-form. DO NOT reverse: the after_that cap at 3, the non-empty first_move.action guard, or CORE REASONING's ordering (identify the blocker before choosing the foothold).

input.project: I need to redesign our pricing page. We currently have three tiers but marketing wants to test a usage-based model instead, and nobody has decided which direction we are actually going. Design, engineering, and sales all have opinions.

output.project_read: You need to redesign the pricing page, but the fundamental model — tiered vs. usage-based — has not been decided, and design, engineering, and sales each have a stake in that decision.

first_move.action: Open a blank doc or note and write down the one question that, if answered, would unblock everything else — something like: 'Does leadership want to commit to usage-based, keep tiers, or run a live test of both?' Then write the names of the two or three people who actually have the authority to answer it.
first_move.why_this: The pricing page cannot be redesigned in a useful direction until the model decision is made, so the real first move is surfacing that decision to the people who can make it.
first_move.done_when: You have one written question and at least one name next to it.
first_move.if_too_hard: Write only the question — skip the names for now.

after_that.action: Send that question to the person most likely to own the decision, framing it as a blocker: 'Before design or engineering can move forward on the pricing page, we need a call on this one thing.'
after_that.done_when: The message is sent and you have noted when you expect a response.

after_that.action: Once the model direction is confirmed, write a single short brief — two to three bullet points per stakeholder group covering what design, engineering, and sales each need the new page to accomplish.
after_that.done_when: Each group has at least one concrete requirement written down and you have shared the doc with them to correct or add to it.

after_that.action: With requirements confirmed, sketch or wireframe the new page structure — just boxes and labels, no polish.
after_that.done_when: You have something you can show to one other person and get a yes or a specific objection.

output.permission_to_stop: Getting the decision question written down and owned is real, necessary work — stopping there is a complete session.

input.project: Write a 6-month marketing plan for our product launch. It needs competitive analysis, channel strategy, a budget, a content calendar, and success metrics. Due in two weeks.

output.project_read: You need to deliver a structured 6-month marketing plan covering five distinct components within two weeks, and the scope is making it hard to find an entry point.

first_move.action: Open a blank document and write five headings: Competitive Analysis, Channel Strategy, Budget, Content Calendar, Success Metrics. Under each heading, write one sentence describing what you already know or assume about that area for this launch.
first_move.why_this: Five sentences is a real first draft of the plan skeleton, and the sentences will surface what you know versus where the gaps are.
first_move.done_when: The document has five headings and at least one sentence under each.
first_move.if_too_hard: Write just the five headings and leave the rest blank, so the structure exists and nothing is hiding inside an undifferentiated pile.

after_that.action: Look at your five sentences and mark the one section where your assumptions feel shakiest or where a wrong call would most hurt the plan.
after_that.done_when: One section is marked and you have written one sentence explaining what you would need to know to feel confident in it.

after_that.action: Draft the Success Metrics section in full: list three to five specific, measurable outcomes the launch will be judged against.
after_that.done_when: Each metric has a name and a target number or threshold, even if the numbers are provisional.

after_that.action: Draft the Channel Strategy section by listing every channel under consideration, then writing one sentence per channel on why it is in or out for this launch.
after_that.done_when: Every channel on your list has a clear in-or-out decision with a stated reason.

output.permission_to_stop: Once the five headings and sentences exist, you have a plan document, not a blank page, and that is enough for this session.

input.project: Clean out my late father's garage. There are decades of tools, boxes, and paperwork and I don't know what to keep.

output.project_read: You are clearing out a garage full of decades of tools, boxes, and paperwork that belonged to your late father, and you are not sure what to keep.

first_move.action: Walk into the garage, pick one surface or corner you can see in full, and count how many distinct categories of things are on it — tools, paper, boxes, unknown. Write the categories down on paper or your phone.
first_move.why_this: Naming what is actually there turns an overwhelming mass into a short, concrete list you can make decisions about one category at a time.
first_move.done_when: You have a written list of the categories visible in that one spot.
first_move.if_too_hard: Stand at the garage door without going in and write down the three largest things you can see from where you are standing.

after_that.action: Return for 20-30 minutes and sort only the items from that first spot into three physical zones: keep, donate, decide-later.
after_that.done_when: Every item from that spot is in one of the three zones and the surface is clear.

after_that.action: Before touching anything that feels significant, photograph the garage from a few angles so you have a record of how it looked.
after_that.done_when: Photos are saved somewhere you can find them.

after_that.action: Pick one category from your list — paperwork, hand tools, or boxes — and make a single rule for it, such as: keep anything with his handwriting, donate duplicates, recycle blank paper.
after_that.done_when: The rule is written down and you can apply it without deciding case by case.

output.permission_to_stop: Getting that list written is a real piece of work done — the garage will still be there, and so will you.
